京胡主要在京劇中作為伴奏樂器，也用於漢劇；演奏時多跟隨演員唱腔並加入裝飾，少換把: The jinghu is mainly an accompanying instrument in Peking opera and is also used in Han opera; in playing it mostly follows the singer's vocal line and adds ornament, rarely shifting position, and it often keeps the melody within a single octave. Its predecessor, the huihu, is still found in the Hui plays within Wu opera. The jinghu is also used prominently on the Japanese band's single “Shinjitsu no Uta”.
京胡屬弦鳴樂器，源出中國，早期稱胡琴、二鼓子，由徽戲中的徽胡發展而來，現婺劇中的: The jinghu is a chordophone from China. It was called the huqin and the erguzi early on, developed from the huihu of the Hui plays, and the Hui plays in Wu opera still use the huihu. It took shape gradually around 1785, at the end of the Qianlong reign of the Qing, along with the pihuang vocal style, and takes its name from serving as the main accompaniment in Peking and Han opera. Early Peking opera favoured a high pitch, with a shorter neck and a smaller soundbox, some covered with python skin and played with a soft bow; after the nineteenth century the hard bow appeared, giving a firmer and brighter sound. In the early twentieth century Peking opera singers prized a round, smooth delivery and kept lowering the pitch, so the neck and the soundbox grew longer with it. Around 1930, when Peking opera flourished as never before, many Beijing instrument shops changed their signs to huqin shops, and famous players hired workers to make and sell instruments.
京胡屬弦鳴樂器，發聲靠弓毛摩擦兩弦，經竹製琴筒與蛇皮膜傳導。琴身主要用竹，琴桿與: The jinghu is a chordophone; it sounds when the bowhair rubs the two strings, and the sound is carried through the bamboo soundbox and the snakeskin membrane. The body is mainly bamboo: the neck and the soundbox are made of purple bamboo, white bamboo or dyed bamboo; one end of the soundbox is covered with snakeskin, and early ones were sometimes covered with python skin. The bridge is of bamboo. The strings were of silk early on and today are mostly steel or nylon. The bowhair runs between the two strings; the source does not state the material of the bow stick or whether it is soft or hard, and other parts such as the tuning pegs are not described in detail either.
京胡是中國弓弦樂器，屬胡琴家族，為其中體積最小、音高最高者。琴桿與琴筒以竹製成，: The jinghu is a Chinese bowed string instrument of the huqin family, the smallest and highest-pitched of them. Its neck and soundbox are of bamboo; the front of the cylindrical resonator is covered with snakeskin, and a bamboo bridge sits between the skin and the strings; the two strings are usually tuned a fifth apart, and the bowhair runs between them. In playing it mostly follows the singer's melody and adds ornament, rarely shifting position, and it often keeps the melody within a single octave. It developed from the huihu of the Hui plays and is one of the main accompanying instruments of Peking and Han opera; its predecessor, the huihu, is still found in the Hui plays of Wu opera.
京胡音色清脆而嘹亮，具有明亮銳利的音質特徵，穿透力強。其音域主要集中在中高音區，: The jinghu's timbre is crisp and piercing, bright and sharp in quality, with strong carrying power. Its range lies mainly in the upper middle register, and it can play many kinds of complex melodic line. The soundbox is covered with snakeskin or python skin, and together with the resonance design of the bamboo neck this gives it an unusual way of resonating: the openings the neck makes in the soundbox form a double-resonance structure that adds colour and penetration to the timbre. Beside the dizi the jinghu is deeper and warmer; beside the erhu its sound is sharper and higher, with some of the softness gone. This is what makes it the leading instrument in Peking opera accompaniment: it blends with the vocal line effectively while keeping an expressive voice of its own.
弦鳴｜321.3 擦弦／輪弦／提琴家族: Chordophone | 321.3 bowed / wheel-bowed / the violin family
用弓在弦上擦奏，透過弓毛與弦的摩擦力使弦震動。將樂器穩定持於身前。左手負責按弦或: The bow is drawn across the strings, and the friction of the bowhair sets them vibrating. Hold the instrument steady in front of the body. The left hand stops the strings or changes the sounding length to control the pitch, and the right hand sets them vibrating. On a chordophone the vibration of the string is amplified by the soundbox. Keep the bowing even and use the weight of the arm rather than the strength of the wrist.
